The proposed method combines Physical Optics, Method of Moments, and Ray Tracing for RCS calculation of large RAM-coated objects.
Reflection coefficients of multilayer RAM structures are computed using either Periodic Method of Moments or a transmission line model.
The method accounts for incidence angle dependence of material reflection properties.
A metallic corner reflector of 0.5 m by 0.5 m with a resistive Frequency Selective Surface coating is used as a benchmark.
FSS patches have side length 9.375 mm, width 0.0625 mm, surface resistance 110 ohm/sq, periodicity 10 mm, and are placed 5 mm above a PEC ground.
The hybrid RT-PO method includes both electric and magnetic surface currents in the scattered field computation.
The Fresnel reflection coefficient matrix Γ is diagonal with components Γ∥ and Γ⊥ for parallel and perpendicular polarizations.
The hybrid method can simulate multiple bounces and reflections between object facets, overcoming classical PO limitations.
RCS results from the hybrid method agree well with full-wave MLFMM simulations for both TE and TM polarizations.
Computation time for the hybrid method is on the order of seconds to minutes, compared to about 2 days for MLFMM full-wave simulations.
Classical PO methods cannot handle electrically large objects coated with RAM efficiently due to computational complexity.
The RT-PO algorithm uses a geometrical check to ensure reflected rays are not obstructed.
The method models the illuminated facets as infinite planes for surface current approximation.
The paper demonstrates the feasibility of using the hybrid method for practical RCS prediction of large coated targets.
The equivalence theorem is applied to analyze metallic surfaces coated with RAM.
The method is validated at microwave frequencies relevant for radar applications.
The reflection coefficient matrix depends on the incidence elevation angle θ.
The hybrid method improves accuracy by combining high-frequency techniques with full-wave MoM calculations for the RAM layer.
The method is suitable for electrically large targets exceeding 30 wavelengths in size.
The benchmark corner reflector is a 90° dihedral with one face coated with RAM.
